content.prompt: Find area bounded by:

children.label: a
children.prompt: $y=2x+1$, the $x$-axis, $x=0$ and $x=3$

spec.description: Rising straight line, unnumbered axes, and shaded region from x=0 to x=3.
spec.mathematics: y=2x+1; 0<=x<=3; region above the x-axis.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question graph; no answer values added.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^3(2x+1)\,dx\\&=[x^2+x]_0^3\\&=(9+3)-0\\&=12\text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $y=4-x^2$, the $x$-axis, $x=-2$ and $x=2$

spec.description: Downward parabola with shaded region between its two x-intercepts; no ticks.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question graph.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-2}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx\\&=\left[4x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{2}\\&=\left(8-\frac83\right)-\left(-8+\frac83\right)\\&=\frac{32}{3}\text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $y=x^2-4$, the $x$-axis, $x=0$ and $x=2$

spec.description: Upward parabola; shaded region between the y-axis and positive x-intercept below the x-axis.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question graph.

answer.worked:
The region is below the $x$-axis.

$$\begin{aligned}A&=-\int_0^2(x^2-4)\,dx\\&=-\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-4x\right]_0^2\\&=-\left(\frac83-8\right)\\&=\frac{16}{3}\text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: $y=x^3-4x$, the $x$-axis, $x=-2$ and $x=-1$

spec.description: Cubic through the origin with shaded region above the axis from x=-2 to x=-1.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question graph.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^3-4x)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-2x^2\right]_{-2}^{-1}\\&=\left(\frac14-2\right)-(4-8)\\&=\frac94\text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: $y=x^2+1$, the $x$-axis, $x=0$ and $x=2$

spec.description: Upward parabola wholly above the x-axis; shaded region from x=0 to x=2.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question graph.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^2(x^2+1)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+x\right]_0^2\\&=\frac83+2\\&=\frac{14}{3}\text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: $y=-x^2$, the $x$-axis, $x=1$ and $x=3$

spec.description: Downward parabola with vertex at the origin and shaded region below the axis between x=1 and x=3.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question graph.

answer.worked:
The region is below the $x$-axis.

$$\begin{aligned}A&=-\int_1^3(-x^2)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^3\\&=9-\frac13\\&=\frac{26}{3}\text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Find an expression for the area of the given region:

spec.description: Parabola with negative region a–b and positive region b–c shaded; vertical boundary at c. No numeric scale is supplied.
spec.mathematics: a<0<b<c; f is negative on (a,b) and positive on (b,c).
spec.answerVisibility: Source graph and boundary labels only.

answer.worked:
The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $b$. Subtract the integral below the axis and add the integral above it.
$$A=-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+\int_b^c f(x)\,dx.$$

spec.description: Cubic-like curve crossing at a, the origin and b; both bounded lobes shaded. No numeric scale is supplied.
spec.mathematics: a<0<b; f is positive on (a,0) and negative on (0,b).
spec.answerVisibility: Source graph and intercept labels only.

answer.worked:
Split at the origin, where the curve changes sign.
$$A=\int_a^0 f(x)\,dx-\int_0^b f(x)\,dx.$$

spec.description: Upward parabola with vertex slightly right of the y-axis; shaded positive region a–c and negative region c–b; vertical boundary at a.
spec.mathematics: a<c<0<b; f is positive on (a,c) and negative on (c,b).
spec.answerVisibility: Source graph and boundary labels only.

answer.worked:
Split at $c$, where the curve changes sign.
$$A=\int_a^c f(x)\,dx-\int_c^b f(x)\,dx.$$

spec.description: Parabola entirely above the x-axis, with shaded area beneath it between vertical boundaries a and b.
spec.mathematics: a<0<b; f is positive throughout [a,b].
spec.answerVisibility: Source graph and boundary labels only.

answer.worked:
The entire shaded region is above the $x$-axis, so no split is needed.
$$A=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

spec.description: Cubic-like curve with intercepts a, c and b; only the negative area from the separate boundary e to b is shaded.
spec.mathematics: a<c<e<0<b; f is negative on (e,b). The portions a–c and c–e are unshaded.
spec.answerVisibility: Source graph and boundary labels only.

answer.worked:
Only the region from $e$ to $b$ is shaded, and it is below the $x$-axis.
$$A=-\int_e^b f(x)\,dx.$$

spec.description: Cubic-like curve with all three regions a–c, c–b and b–d shaded; vertical right boundary at d.
spec.mathematics: a<c<0<b<d; f is positive on (a,c), negative on (c,b), and positive on (b,d).
spec.answerVisibility: Source graph and boundary labels only.

answer.worked:
Split at $c$ and $b$, where the curve changes sign. Add the positive integrals and subtract the negative integral.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_a^c f(x)\,dx-\int_c^b f(x)\,dx\\&\quad+\int_b^d f(x)\,dx.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the area bounded by $y=x^2-x-2$, the $x$-axis, and lines $x=-2$ and $x=1$.

spec.description: Equation-driven upward-opening parabola, double-ended axes, curve-end arrowheads and no ticks. Light green shading identifies the requested area; green vertical boundaries mark the interval endpoints.
spec.mathematics: y=x^2-x-2, roots -1 and 2; shaded interval [-2,1], with a positive region on [-2,-1] and a negative region on [-1,1].
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied curve and shaded region appear; no calculated roots, values or answers are labelled.

answer.worked:
Find the $x$-intercepts.
$$\begin{align*}
x^2-x-2&=0\\
(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\
x&=-1,\ 2
\end{align*}$$
Only $x=-1$ lies inside the interval $[-2,1]$.
$$\begin{align*}
A&=\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^2-x-2)\,dx+\left|\int_{-1}^{1}(x^2-x-2)\,dx\right|\\
A&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}-2x\right]_{-2}^{-1}+\left|\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}-2x\right]_{-1}^{1}\right|\\
A&=\left(\frac76-\left(-\frac23\right)\right)+\left| -\frac{13}{6}-\frac76\right|\\
A&=\frac{11}{6}+\left|-\frac{10}{3}\right|\\
A&=\frac{31}{6}\text{ units}^2
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the area enclosed between the $x$-axis and $y=x(x+1)(x-2)$.

spec.description: Equation-driven cubic with lower-left and upper-right arrowheads, double-ended axes and no ticks. Both bounded lobes are shaded light green.
spec.mathematics: y=x(x+1)(x-2), roots -1, 0 and 2. Positive lobe on [-1,0], larger negative lobe on [0,2].
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and shaded regions appear; roots and calculated areas are not labelled.

answer.worked:
Find the $x$-intercepts.
$$\begin{align*}
x(x+1)(x-2)&=0\\
x&=-1,\ 0,\ 2
\end{align*}$$
Split the enclosed area at $x=0$.
$$\begin{align*}
x(x+1)(x-2)&=x^3-x^2-2x\\
A&=\int_{-1}^{0}(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx+\left|\int_{0}^{2}(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx\right|\\
A&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left|\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{0}^{2}\right|\\
A&=0-\left(\frac14+\frac13-1\right)+\left|4-\frac83-4-0\right|\\
A&=\frac5{12}+\left|-\frac83\right|\\
A&=\frac{37}{12}\text{ units}^2
\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: By evaluating $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}(x+1)\,dx$, find the area of the shaded region above the $x$-axis.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A_{\text{above}}&=\int_{-1}^{2}(x+1)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^{2}\\&=(2+2)-\left(\frac12-1\right)\\&=\frac92\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: By evaluating $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{-1}(x+1)\,dx$, find the area of the shaded region below the $x$-axis.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}I&=\int_{-3}^{-1}(x+1)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-3}^{-1}\\&=\left(\frac12-1\right)-\left(\frac92-3\right)\\&=-2.\end{align*}$$
The region is below the $x$-axis, so its area is $|-2|=2\text{ units}^2$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence find the area of the entire shaded region.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A_{\text{total}}&=\frac92+2\\&=\frac{13}{2}\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Find $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{2}(x+1)\,dx$, and explain why this integral does not give the area of the shaded region.

answer.short: $\dfrac52$. The integral gives the area above the $x$-axis minus the area below it, rather than the total area.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\int_{-3}^{2}(x+1)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-3}^{2}\\&=(2+2)-\left(\frac92-3\right)\\&=\frac52.\end{align*}$$
The region below the $x$-axis contributes negatively. Thus the integral gives $\frac92-2=\frac52$, whereas the total area is $\frac92+2=\frac{13}{2}\text{ units}^2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: By evaluating $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{1}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx$, find the area of the shaded region below the $x$-axis.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-3}^{1}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+x^2-3x\right]_{-3}^{1}\\&=\left(\frac13+1-3\right)-\left(-9+9+9\right)\\&=-\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}$$
The region is below the $x$-axis, so its area is $\left|-\dfrac{32}{3}\right|=10\dfrac23\text{ units}^2$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: By evaluating $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx$, find the area of the shaded region above the $x$-axis.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{1}^{2}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+x^2-3x\right]_{1}^{2}\\&=\left(\frac83+4-6\right)-\left(\frac13+1-3\right)\\&=\frac73\\&=2\frac13\text{ units}^2.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{32}{3}+\frac73\\&=13\text{ units}^2.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Find $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{2}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx$, and explain why this integral does not give the area of the shaded region.

answer.short: $-8\dfrac13$. This is the area above the $x$-axis minus the area below it, rather than the total area.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-3}^{2}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx&=\int_{-3}^{1}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx+\int_{1}^{2}(x^2+2x-3)\,dx\\&=-\frac{32}{3}+\frac73\\&=-\frac{25}{3}\\&=-8\frac13.\end{aligned}$$
The integral subtracts the area below the $x$-axis from the area above it. The total area requires both areas to be added as positive values.

children.label: b
children.prompt: By evaluating $\displaystyle\int_0^2(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx$, find the area of the shaded region below the $x$-axis.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^2(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\\
&=\left(4-\frac83-4\right)-0\\
&=-\frac83.
\end{aligned}$$
The region is below the $x$-axis, so its area is $\left|-\dfrac83\right|=2\dfrac23\ \text{u}^2$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: By evaluating $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx$, find the area of the shaded region above the $x$-axis.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}
A_{\text{above}}&=\int_{-1}^0(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^0\\
&=0-\left(\frac14+\frac13-1\right)\\
&=\frac5{12}\ \text{u}^2.
\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}

&=\frac{37}{12}\\

\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Find $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^2(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx$, and explain why this integral does not give the area of the shaded region.

answer.short: $-2\dfrac14\ \text{u}^2$. This is the area above the $x$-axis minus the area below it, not the total area.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1}^2(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^2\\
&=\left(4-\frac83-4\right)-\left(\frac14+\frac13-1\right)\\
&=-\frac83+\frac5{12}\\
&=-\frac94=-2\frac14\ \text{u}^2.
\end{aligned}$$
The integral counts the region below the $x$-axis negatively. It gives the area above the axis minus the area below it, whereas total area adds both positive areas.

content.prompt: In each part, find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the function and the $x$-axis between the specified values. Areas above and below the $x$-axis must be calculated separately. A sketch of the curve will help.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $y=x^2$, between $x=-3$ and $x=2$

answer.worked:
$y=x^2\geq0$, so the entire region is above the $x$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-3}^{2}x^2\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-3}^{2}\\&=\frac83-(-9)\\&=\frac{35}{3}=11\frac23\text{ units}^2.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $y=2x^3$, between $x=-4$ and $x=1$

answer.worked:
The zero is $x=0$. The curve is below the $x$-axis on $[-4,0]$ and above it on $[0,1]$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{below}}&=-\int_{-4}^{0}2x^3\,dx\\&=-\left[\frac{x^4}{2}\right]_{-4}^{0}\\&=-(0-128)=128.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{above}}&=\int_{0}^{1}2x^3\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^4}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}\\&=\frac12.\end{aligned}$$
$$A=128+\frac12=128\frac12\text{ units}^2.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $y=3x(x-2)$, between $x=0$ and $x=2$

answer.worked:
The zeros are $x=0$ and $x=2$. The curve is below the $x$-axis on $(0,2)$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=-\int_0^2(3x^2-6x)\,dx\\&=-[x^3-3x^2]_0^2\\&=-[(8-12)-0]\\&=4\text{ units}^2.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: $y=x-3$, between $x=-1$ and $x=4$

answer.worked:
The zero is $x=3$. The curve is below the $x$-axis on $[-1,3]$ and above it on $[3,4]$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{below}}&=-\int_{-1}^{3}(x-3)\,dx\\&=-\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-3x\right]_{-1}^{3}\\&=-\left[\left(\frac92-9\right)-\left(\frac12+3\right)\right]\\&=8.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{above}}&=\int_3^4(x-3)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-3x\right]_3^4\\&=(8-12)-\left(\frac92-9\right)=\frac12.\end{aligned}$$
$$A=8+\frac12=8\frac12\text{ units}^2.$$

$y=x^3-7x+6$, with zeros at $x=-3,1,2$.
On $(-3,1)$, checking $x=0$ gives $y=6>0$, so the curve is above the $x$-axis. On $(1,2)$, checking $x=1.5$ gives $y=-1.125<0$, so it is below.
$$F(x)=\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{7x^2}{2}+6x.$$
$$F(-3)=-\frac{117}{4},\qquad F(1)=\frac{11}{4},\qquad F(2)=2.$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{above}}&=F(1)-F(-3)\\&=\frac{11}{4}+\frac{117}{4}\\&=32.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{below}}&=-[F(2)-F(1)]\\&=-\left[2-\frac{11}{4}\right]\\&=\frac34.\end{aligned}$$
$$A=32+\frac34=32\frac34\text{ units}^2.$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: $y=-2x(x+1)$, between $x=-2$ and $x=2$

answer.worked:
$y=-2x(x+1)=-2x^2-2x$, with zeros at $x=-1$ and $x=0$.
On $(-2,-1)$, checking $x=-1.5$ gives $y=-1.5$, below the $x$-axis. On $(-1,0)$, checking $x=-0.5$ gives $y=0.5$, above. On $(0,2)$, checking $x=1$ gives $y=-4$, below.
$$F(x)=-\frac{2x^3}{3}-x^2.$$
$$F(-2)=\frac43,\quad F(-1)=-\frac13,\quad F(0)=0,\quad F(2)=-\frac{28}{3}.$$
Below on $[-2,-1]$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=-[F(-1)-F(-2)]\\&=-\left[-\frac13-\frac43\right]=\frac53.\end{aligned}$$
Above on $[-1,0]$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=F(0)-F(-1)\\&=0-\left(-\frac13\right)=\frac13.\end{aligned}$$
Below on $[0,2]$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_3&=-[F(2)-F(0)]\\&=-\left[-\frac{28}{3}-0\right]=\frac{28}{3}.\end{aligned}$$
$$A=\frac53+\frac13+\frac{28}{3}=\frac{34}{3}\text{ units}^2.$$

content.prompt:
Look carefully for any symmetries that will simplify the calculation.
Find the area of the region bounded by the given curve and the $x$-axis.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $y=x^7$, for $-2\le x\le 2$

answer.worked:
$y=x^7$ is odd, so the areas on $[-2,0]$ and $[0,2]$ are equal. On $[0,2]$, the curve is above the $x$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^2x^7\,dx\\&=2\left[\frac{x^8}{8}\right]_0^2\\&=2\left(\frac{256}{8}-0\right)\\&=64\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

The function is odd, so its graph is symmetric about the origin. Its zeros are $x=-4,0,4$.
On $[0,4]$, $x(x-4)(x+4)\le0$. For example, at $x=2$, $y=2(-2)(6)=-24$, below the $x$-axis.
By symmetry,
$$A=2\left(-\int_0^4(x^3-16x)\,dx\right).$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4(x^3-16x)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-8x^2\right]_0^4\\&=(64-128)-0\\&=-64\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2(64)\\&=128\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

The function is even, so its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. Its zeros are $x=-3,0,3$.
On $[0,3]$, the curve is on or below the $x$-axis. For example, at $x=1$, $y=1-9=-8$.
By symmetry,
$$A=2\left(-\int_0^3(x^4-9x^2)\,dx\right).$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^3(x^4-9x^2)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^5}{5}-3x^3\right]_0^3\\&=\left(\frac{243}{5}-81\right)-0\\&=-\frac{162}{5}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\left(\frac{162}{5}\right)\\&=\frac{324}{5}\\&=64\frac45\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: The rate of flow of water into a dam is given by $R=500+20t\ \mathrm{L\,h^{-1}}$. If there is $15\,000\ \mathrm{L}$ of water initially in the dam, how much water will there be in the dam after 10 hours?

answer.worked:
Let $V$ be the volume of water in litres, with $t$ measured in hours.

$$\begin{align*}V&=\int(500+20t)\,dt\\V&=500t+10t^2+C\end{align*}$$
Using $V=15\,000$ when $t=0$ gives $C=15\,000$.

$$\begin{align*}V(10)&=500(10)+10(10^2)+15\,000\\V(10)&=21\,000\ \mathrm{L}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: $x=y-5$, between $y=0$ and $y=6$

answer.worked:
$x=y-5$ is zero at $y=5$. For $0\le y<5$, $x<0$ (left of the $y$-axis). For $5<y\le6$, $x>0$ (right of the $y$-axis).

Left:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{left}}&=-\int_0^5(y-5)\,dy\\&=-\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-5y\right]_0^5\\&=-\left(\frac{25}{2}-25\right)\\&=\frac{25}{2}\end{align*}$$
Right:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{right}}&=\int_5^6(y-5)\,dy\\&=\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-5y\right]_5^6\\&=(18-30)-\left(\frac{25}{2}-25\right)\\&=\frac12\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{total}}&=\frac{25}{2}+\frac12\\&=13\text{ u}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $x=3-y$, between $y=2$ and $y=5$

answer.worked:
$x=3-y$ is zero at $y=3$. For $2\le y<3$, $x>0$ (right of the $y$-axis). For $3<y\le5$, $x<0$ (left of the $y$-axis).

Right:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{right}}&=\int_2^3(3-y)\,dy\\&=\left[3y-\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_2^3\\&=\left(9-\frac92\right)-(6-2)\\&=\frac12\end{align*}$$
Left:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{left}}&=-\int_3^5(3-y)\,dy\\&=-\left[3y-\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_3^5\\&=-\left[\left(15-\frac{25}{2}\right)-\left(9-\frac92\right)\right]\\&=2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{total}}&=\frac12+2\\&=\frac52\\&=2\frac12\text{ u}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $x=y^2$, between $y=-1$ and $y=3$.

answer.worked:
$x=y^2\geq0$, so the entire region from $y=-1$ to $y=3$ is to the right of the $y$-axis.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_{-1}^{3}y^2\,dy\\A&=\left[\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{3}\\A&=\frac{27}{3}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\\A&=9+\frac{1}{3}\\A&=9\frac{1}{3}\text{ u}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: $x=(y-1)(y+1)$, between $y=3$ and $y=0$.

answer.worked:
$x=(y-1)(y+1)=y^2-1$, with zeros at $y=\pm1$. The curve is to the right of the $y$-axis when $|y|>1$ and to the left when $|y|<1$.
Between $y=0$ and $y=1$, $x<0$. Between $y=1$ and $y=3$, $x>0$.
Left region:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{left}}&=-\int_0^1(y^2-1)\,dy\\A_{\text{left}}&=-\left[\frac{y^3}{3}-y\right]_0^1\\A_{\text{left}}&=-\left(\frac13-1\right)\\A_{\text{left}}&=\frac23.\end{align*}$$
Right region:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{right}}&=\int_1^3(y^2-1)\,dy\\A_{\text{right}}&=\left[\frac{y^3}{3}-y\right]_1^3\\A_{\text{right}}&=(9-3)-\left(\frac13-1\right)\\A_{\text{right}}&=\frac{20}{3}.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac23+\frac{20}{3}\\A&=7\frac13\text{ u}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the $x$-intercept and the $y$-intercepts.

answer.worked:
For the $x$-intercept, set $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=16(2-x)\\x&=2.\end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercept is $(2,0)$.

For the $y$-intercepts, set $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y^2&=32\\y&=\pm4\sqrt2.\end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercepts are $(0,4\sqrt2)$ and $(0,-4\sqrt2)$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^2 4\sqrt{2-x}\,dx\\A&=4\left[-\frac{2(2-x)^{3/2}}{3}\right]_0^2\\A&=4\left[0+\frac{2(2\sqrt2)}{3}\right]\\A&=\frac{16\sqrt2}{3}\text{ units}^2.\end{aligned}$$

$$x=2-\frac{y^2}{16}$$

answer.worked: The interval from $a$ to $b$ has length $b-a$ and is divided into $n$ equal intervals, so $h=\dfrac{b-a}{n}$.

$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=\frac{h}{2}\bigl(f(x_1)+f(x_2)\bigr)\\&=\frac{b-a}{2n}\bigl(f(x_1)+f(x_2)\bigr).\end{aligned}$$

answer.short: $\pi\approx3.0$ (1 d.p.). The curve is concave down, so the trapezoidal rule underestimates the quarter-circle area.
answer.worked:
The curve $y=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ is the upper half of the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$. Between $x=0$ and $x=1$, the area is one quarter of the unit circle.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi}{4}&\approx0.7489\\\pi&\approx4\times0.7489\\&=2.9956\\&\approx3.0\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

The curve is concave down, so each trapezium lies below the curve. The area estimate is too small, and multiplying it by $4$ gives an approximation less than $\pi$.

answer.worked:

children.prompt: Differentiate $x^2+1$, and hence find the area under the graph $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$, between $x=0$ and $x=2$. Give the exact area and an approximation to 3 decimal places.

answer.worked:
$$\frac{d}{dx}(x^2+1)=2x.$$
Since the numerator is half the derivative of the denominator,
$$\int\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx=\frac12\ln(x^2+1)+C.$$
The curve is non-negative on $0\le x\le2$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_0^2\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx\\&=\left[\frac12\ln(x^2+1)\right]_0^2\\&=\frac12\ln5-\frac12\ln1\\&=\frac12\ln5\\&\approx0.805\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
$$\frac{d}{dx}(x^2+2x+3)=2x+2=2(x+1).$$
Since the numerator is half the derivative of the denominator,
$$\int\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+3}\,dx=\frac12\ln(x^2+2x+3)+C.$$

$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_0^1\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+3}\,dx\\&=\left[\frac12\ln(x^2+2x+3)\right]_0^1\\&=\frac12\ln6-\frac12\ln3\\&=\frac12\ln2\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use the trapezoidal rule with four subintervals to approximate the area between the curve $y=\ln x$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=1$ and $x=5$. Answer correct to four decimal places.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}h&=\frac{5-1}{4}=1\\x&=1,2,3,4,5\\f(x)&=\ln x\\A&\approx\frac{1}{2}\left(\ln1+2(\ln2+\ln3+\ln4)+\ln5\right)\\A&\approx3.9828\text{ units}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Differentiate $y=x\log_e x$. Hence find the exact value of the area, and approximate it correct to four decimal places.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=x\left(\frac1x\right)+\ln x\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\ln x+1\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x-x+C\\A&=\left[x\ln x-x\right]_1^5\\A&=(5\ln5-5)-(0-1)\\A&=5\ln5-4\\A&\approx4.0472\text{ units}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Is the estimate greater than or less than the exact value? Explain how the graph could have predicted this.

answer.short: Less than the exact value: the graph is concave down, so the trapezoidal chords lie below the curve.
answer.worked: The estimate is less than the exact value. For $y=\ln x$, $y''=-\dfrac{1}{x^2}<0$ on $[1,5]$. The graph is concave down, so the chords forming the tops of the trapezia lie below the curve.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the curves $y=\dfrac{6}{x}$ and $y=x^2-6x+11$ intersect when $x=1$, $2$ and $3$.

answer.short: The points $(1,6)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$ lie on both curves.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Graph these two curves and shade the two areas enclosed by them.

answer.short: Shade the regions between the curves for $1\le x\le2$ and $2\le x\le3$.
answer.worked: The curves intersect at $(1,6)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$. The parabola is above the hyperbola on $1<x<2$, and the hyperbola is above the parabola on $2<x<3$. Shade these two enclosed regions.

spec.description: Authored solution graph with a solid reciprocal curve, dashed parabola, labelled intersections and the two enclosed regions shaded light blue. The source provides blank drawing space.
spec.mathematics: y=6/x and y=(x-3)^2+2 intersect at (1,6), (2,3), (3,2). The parabola is higher on (1,2); the reciprocal curve is higher on (2,3).
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; no graph or axes are supplied in the student question.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the total area enclosed by the two curves.

answer.worked:
On $[1,2]$, the parabola is above the hyperbola. On $[2,3]$, the hyperbola is above the parabola.

$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_1^2\left(x^2-6x+11-\frac6x\right)\,dx+\int_2^3\left(\frac6x-x^2+6x-11\right)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-3x^2+11x-6\ln x\right]_1^2+\left[6\ln x-\frac{x^3}{3}+3x^2-11x\right]_2^3\\&=\left(\frac{13}{3}-6\ln2\right)+\left(6\ln\frac32-\frac73\right)\\&=2-6\ln\frac43\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Sketch the region bounded by the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$, and by the vertical lines $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.short: See sketch. The required region lies between the two curves for $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{\pi}{6}$, with $\cos x$ above $\sin x$.
answer.worked: Sketch $y=\sin x$ through $(0,0)$ and $y=\cos x$ through $(0,1)$. Draw the vertical boundaries $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$. Between these boundaries, $\cos x\ge\sin x$; the required region lies between the curves.

spec.description: Unshaded sine and cosine curves on common arrowed axes, extending beyond dashed vertical boundaries. Curve-name labels are absent, as in the source. Ordinary axes, guides and labels use house black.
spec.mathematics: y=sin(x) and y=cos(x); boundaries x=-pi/2 and x=pi/6. Cosine is above sine throughout the bounded interval.
spec.answerVisibility: Answer only; no graph appears in the student prompt.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the area of the region in part a.

answer.worked:
On $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{6}\right]$, $\cos x\ge\sin x$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx\\&=\left[\sin x+\cos x\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}\\&=\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-(-1+0)\\&=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{2}\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show by substitution that $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos 2x$ meet at $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.short: At $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, both functions equal $-1$. At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, both functions equal $\dfrac12$.
answer.worked:
At $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&=-1,\\\cos\left(2\times-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&=\cos(-\pi)\\&=-1.\end{align*}$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin\frac{\pi}{6}&=\frac12,\\\cos\left(2\times\frac{\pi}{6}\right)&=\cos\frac{\pi}{3}\\&=\frac12.\end{align*}$$
The two functions have the same value at each specified $x$-coordinate, so they meet at both points.

The supplied equation-solving working also gives:
$$\begin{align*}\sin x&=\cos 2x\\\sin x&=1-2\sin^2x\\2\sin^2x+\sin x-1&=0\\(2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\sin x=\dfrac12$ or $\sin x=-1$, giving $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ respectively in the interval used in part b.

children.label: b
children.prompt: On the same number plane, sketch $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos 2x$, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.short: The curves meet at $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac12\right)$. Between these points, $y=\cos 2x$ lies above $y=\sin x$. See sketch.
answer.worked: $y=\sin x$ increases from $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-1\right)$ through $(0,0)$ to $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac12\right)$. The curve $y=\cos 2x$ rises from the first intersection to its maximum $(0,1)$, then falls to the second intersection. Draw both curves on the same axes.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence find the area of the region bounded by the two curves.

answer.worked:
On $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]$, $\cos 2x\ge\sin x$.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}(\cos 2x-\sin x)\,dx\\&=\left[\frac12\sin 2x+\cos x\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}\\&=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{4}+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-(0+0)\\&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Use symmetry to help evaluate:

children.label: a
children.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{-4\pi}^{4\pi}\sin 3x\,dx$

answer.worked:
$\sin 3x$ is odd and the limits are symmetric about zero.
$$\int_{-4\pi}^{4\pi}\sin 3x\,dx=0.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{-2\pi}^{2\pi}\cos^2x\sin^3x\,dx$

answer.worked:
$\cos^2x$ is even and $\sin^3x$ is odd, so their product is odd. The limits are symmetric about zero.
$$\int_{-2\pi}^{2\pi}\cos^2x\sin^3x\,dx=0.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{-5\pi/2}^{5\pi/2}\cos x\,dx$

answer.worked:
$\cos x$ is even.
$$\begin{align*}\int_{-5\pi/2}^{5\pi/2}\cos x\,dx&=2\int_0^{5\pi/2}\cos x\,dx\\&=2[\sin x]_0^{5\pi/2}\\&=2\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{2}\right)\\&=2.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sec^2\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\,dx$

answer.worked:
$\sec^2(x/3)$ is even.
$$\begin{align*}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sec^2\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\,dx&=2\int_0^\pi\sec^2\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\,dx\\&=2\left[3\tan\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^\pi\\&=6\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=6\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(3+2x+\sin x)\,dx$

answer.worked:
$2x$ and $\sin x$ are odd, so each contributes zero over these symmetric limits. The constant function $3$ is even.
$$\begin{align*}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}(3+2x+\sin x)\,dx&=2\int_0^\pi3\,dx\\&=2[3x]_0^\pi\\&=6\pi.\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(\sin 2x+\cos 3x+3x^2)\,dx$

answer.worked:
$\sin 2x$ is odd, so it contributes zero. Both $\cos 3x$ and $3x^2$ are even.
$$\begin{align*}2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos 3x\,dx&=2\left[\frac13\sin 3x\right]_0^{\pi/2}\\&=\frac23(-1)\\&=-\frac23.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}2\int_0^{\pi/2}3x^2\,dx&=[2x^3]_0^{\pi/2}\\&=\frac{\pi^3}{4}.\end{align*}$$
$$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(\sin 2x+\cos 3x+3x^2)\,dx=-\frac23+\frac{\pi^3}{4}.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\sqrt{2}\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sin x+\cos x$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\sqrt{2}\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\sqrt{2}\left(\sin x\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\cos x\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\&=\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\\&=\sin x+\cos x.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact area under one arch of the curve $y=\sin x+\cos x$.

answer.worked:
One arch of $y=\sin x+\cos x=\sqrt{2}\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ lies above the $x$-axis from $x=-\frac{\pi}{4}$ to $x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$.

$$\begin{align*}A&=\int_{-\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}\sqrt{2}\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\,dx\\&=\left[-\sqrt{2}\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]_{-\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}\\&=\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}\\&=2\sqrt{2}\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Similarly, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^N 2xe^{-x^2}\,dx$, and find its limit as $N\to\infty$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
\int_0^N 2xe^{-x^2}\,dx&=\left[-e^{-x^2}\right]_0^N\\
&=-e^{-N^2}-(-1)\\
&=1-e^{-N^2}.
\end{align*}$$
As $N\to\infty$, $e^{-N^2}\to0$.
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_0^N 2xe^{-x^2}\,dx=1.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^n(1+\sin 2\pi x)\,dx=n$, for all positive integers $n$.

answer.worked:
For every positive integer $n$, $\cos 2\pi n=1$.
$$\begin{align*}\int_0^n(1+\sin 2\pi x)\,dx&=\left[x-\frac{1}{2\pi}\cos 2\pi x\right]_0^n\\&=\left(n-\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)-\left(0-\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)\\&=n.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Sketch $y=1+\sin 2\pi x$, and interpret the result geometrically.

answer.short: The curve oscillates between $y=0$ and $y=2$ about $y=1$, with period $1$. Over $0\le x\le n$, deviations above and below $y=1$ cancel, so the area under the curve is $n$ square units.
answer.worked:
The curve $y=1+\sin 2\pi x$ oscillates about $y=1$ with period $1$, and passes through $(0,1)$. Its maximum value is $2$ and its minimum value is $0$.

For positive integer $n$, the interval $0\le x\le n$ contains $n$ complete periods. The positive and negative deviations from $y=1$ cancel, so the area under the curve equals the area of a rectangle $n$ units long and $1$ unit high:
$$A=n\times1=n\text{ square units}.$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Using the fact that $\sin x<x<\tan x$ for $0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$, explain why $x^2\sin x<x^3<x^2\tan x$ for $0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$.

answer.short: Since $x^2>0$, multiplying the given inequality by $x^2$ preserves its direction: $x^2\sin x<x^3<x^2\tan x$.
answer.worked:
For $0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin x<x<\tan x$ and $x^2>0$. Multiplying through by $x^2$ gives
$$x^2\sin x<x^3<x^2\tan x.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}x^2\sin x\,dx<\frac{\pi^4}{4^5}<\int_0^{\pi/4}x^2\tan x\,dx$.

answer.worked:
Integrating the inequality from part a over $0\le x\le\frac{\pi}{4}$ preserves strict inequalities because they are strict throughout the interior:
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{\pi/4}x^2\sin x\,dx&<\left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\pi/4}<\int_0^{\pi/4}x^2\tan x\,dx\\
\int_0^{\pi/4}x^2\sin x\,dx&<\frac{\pi^4}{4^5}<\int_0^{\pi/4}x^2\tan x\,dx.
\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Given that $y=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}$, show that $y'=-\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}y&=(1+\sin x)^{-1}\\y'&=-(1+\sin x)^{-2}\cos x\\&=-\frac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence explain why the function $y=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}$ is decreasing for $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

answer.short: On $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos x>0$ and $(1+\sin x)^2>0$, so $y'<0$. Hence $y$ is decreasing.
answer.worked: For $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos x>0$ and $(1+\sin x)^2>0$. Therefore $y'=-\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}<0$, so $y$ is decreasing.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Sketch the curve for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and hence show that $\dfrac{\pi}{4}<\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}\,dx<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

answer.short: The curve decreases from $(0,1)$ to $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac12\right)$ and flattens at its right endpoint. Its area lies strictly between the areas of rectangles of width $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and heights $\dfrac12$ and $1$, so $\dfrac{\pi}{4}<\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}\,dx<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
answer.worked:
Since $y$ is decreasing on $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$,
$$\begin{aligned}y\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&\le y(x)\le y(0),\\\frac12&\le\frac{1}{1+\sin x}\le1.\end{aligned}$$
Integrating gives
$$\begin{aligned}\frac12\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&\le\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{1+\sin x}\,dx\le1\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right).\end{aligned}$$
The curve lies strictly between the two horizontal bounds for $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so both area inequalities are strict:
$$\frac{\pi}{4}<\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{1+\sin x}\,dx<\frac{\pi}{2}.$$

Idea: Compare the exponential sum's area with the existing exponential difference's total area.
Why: This connects symmetry and the gap between the curves on the positive half-interval.
Proposed addition: Append (e) Find the area between y=e^x+e^(−x) and the x-axis for −3≤x≤3. Answer: 2(e³−e^(−3)) square units. (f) How much greater is this than the area found in part (d)? entries.description: Apply \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)\), where \(F(x)\) is a primitive of \(f(x)\), to calculate definite integrals and solve related theoretical problems involving functions within the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course

Describe, in the case where \(f(x)\geq0\) for all values of \(x\) in the interval \(a\leq x\leq b\), the area bounded by the graph of the continuous function \(y=f(x)\), the \(x\)-axis and the lines \(x=a\) and \(x=b\), as \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\)

Recognise, in the case where \(f(x)\leq0\) for all values of \(x\) in the interval \(a\leq x\leq b\), the area bounded by the graph of the continuous function \(y=f(x)\), the \(x\)-axis and the lines \(x=a\) and \(x=b\), as \(\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right|\) or \(-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\)

Conclude, for a continuous function \(y=f(x)\) on the interval \(a\leq x\leq b\), that \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\) (area of regions between curve and \(x\)-axis lying above the \(x\)-axis) − (area of regions between curve and the \(x\)-axis lying below the \(x\)-axis)

Use definite integrals to solve problems involving the areas of regions bounded by the graph of the continuous function \(y=f(x)\), the \(x\)-axis and the lines \(x=a\) and \(x=b\), in cases where \(f(x)\geq0\) throughout \(a\leq x\leq b\), \(f(x)\leq0\) throughout \(a\leq x\leq b\) or where \(f(x)\) changes sign in the interval \(a\leq x\leq b\), with or without the graph provided

Use definite integrals to solve problems involving the areas of regions bounded by the graph of the continuous function \(y=f(x)\), the \(y\)-axis and the lines \(y=a\) and \(y=b\), in cases where \(x\geq0\) throughout \(a\leq y\leq b\), \(x\leq0\) throughout \(a\leq y\leq b\) or where \(x\) changes sign in the interval \(a\leq y\leq b\) with or without the graph provided

Use the fact that the graphs of \(y=a^x\) and \(y=\log_a x\) are reflections of each other in the line \(y=x\) to solve problems involving areas between the \(x\)-axis or \(y\)-axis and a curve involving either an exponential or logarithmic function
Recognise and use the result, where \(f(x)\) is continuous on the interval \(a\leq x\leq c\), \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+\int_b^c f(x)\,dx=\int_a^c f(x)\,dx\) for all \(c\) such that \(a\leq b\leq c\)
Define and use the result \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=-\int_b^a f(x)\,dx\), where \(f(x)\) is continuous on the interval \(a\leq x\leq b\)
Recognise and use symmetry, particularly of odd and even functions, to simplify and solve integration problems
Use the Trapezoidal rule to approximate integrals
Use an online computational application to evaluate definite and indefinite integrals involving functions within and beyond the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course

x = (y − 1)(y + 1) = y² − 1, zeros at y = ±1. Right of y-axis when |y| > 1, left when |y| < 1. From y = 0 to y = 1, x < 0 (left). From y = 1 to y = 3, x > 0 (right). Accuracy of Trapezoidal Rule

The more intervals you use, the more accurate the estimate.
If the curve is concave up in the region, the trapezoidal rule overestimates the integral.
If the curve is concave down in the region, the trapezoidal rule underestimates the integral.
If the curve is linear, the trapezoidal rule gives the exact value of the integral.

entries.presentation: Response requires numerical working and a written explanation.

entries.description:
Supplied blue working: y = √(1 − x²) is the upper half of the unit circle x² + y² = 1.
So A ≈ 0.7489 represents one quarter of a unit circle: (1/4)π(1)².
So π ≈ 4 × 0.7489 ≈ 3.0 (1 d.p.).
Since the semicircle is concave down, the approximation is less than π.

entries.description: Two-part question on a trigonometric identity and the exact area under one arch.
Show that √2 sin(x + π/4) = sin x + cos x.

Supplied working: √2 sin(x + π/4)
= √2(sin x cos(π/4) + cos x sin(π/4))
= √2((sin x + cos x)/√2)
= sin x + cos x.
entries.presentation: Blue teacher answer, separate from the student prompt; successive equality lines.

entries.description: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact area under one arch of the curve y = sin x + cos x.

Supplied answer: One arch of y = sin x + cos x = √2 sin(x + π/4), from x = −π/4 to x = 3π/4.
∫ from −π/4 to 3π/4 of √2 sin(x + π/4) dx = [−√2 cos(x + π/4)] from −π/4 to 3π/4
= √2 + √2
= 2√2 u².
entries.presentation: Blue teacher answer; explanatory line followed by successive integration steps.

entries.description: Similarly, evaluate ∫₀ᴺ 2xe^(−x²) dx, and find its limit as N → ∞.

Supplied working: ∫₀ᴺ 2xe^(−x²) dx = [−e^(−x²)]₀ᴺ = 1 − e^(−N²).
As N → ∞, e^(−N²) → 0.
Limit = 1.

= (n − 1/(2π)) − (0 − 1/(2π))
